title: THE MOST TERRIFYING WORDS JESUS SPOKE TO PEOPLE WHO THOUGHT THEY WERE FIRST
paragraphs: THE MOST TERRIFYING WORDS JESUS SPOKE TO PEOPLE WHO THOUGHT THEY WERE FIRST
“The last will be first, and the first last.” — Matthew 19:30; 20:16
What if you spent your entire life believing you were ahead of everyone else spiritually… only to discover that the people you looked down on were entering the Kingdom ahead of you?
Imagine standing before Jesus.

You have served in church. You have given offerings. You have attended worship services when others stayed home. You have defended the faith, memorized Scripture, and tried to live a respectable Christian life.
Then you notice someone standing nearby.
Someone whose past was a scandal.

Someone who wasted years in rebellion. Someone whose marriage collapsed because of terrible choices. Someone who once mocked Christianity. Someone whose sins became public while yours remained carefully hidden.
And somehow, that person is welcomed with the same astonishing grace you received.
Something inside you whispers:
“But Lord… I served You longer.”
And suddenly, you understand why Jesus told a story about workers, wages, and a vineyard.
Because sometimes the greatest obstacle between a religious person and the heart of God is not an obvious sin.
It is the secret belief that grace should reward us more generously than it rewards someone else.
And Jesus knew exactly how to expose it.
The story begins with a young man who seemed to have everything.
He was wealthy. Respectable. Morally serious. He approached Jesus with a question that sounded sincere: “What good thing shall I do, that I may have eternal life?” (Matthew 19:16, KJV).
He was looking for something he could do.
Something he could accomplish.
Perhaps one more act of obedience that would secure his future.
But Jesus eventually touched the one place the man was unwilling to surrender.
His possessions.
Jesus told him to sell what he had, give to the poor, and follow Him. The young man went away sorrowful because he had great possessions (Matthew 19:21–22).
Notice what happened.
He came looking for eternal life.
He walked away grieving because following Jesus would cost him something he treasured more.
His wealth was not merely something he owned. In that moment, it revealed something that owned his heart.
And before we judge him, we should ask ourselves an uncomfortable question.
What would Jesus have to touch in our lives to make us walk away sorrowful?
Our reputation?
Our relationships?
Our hidden habits?
Our bank accounts?
Our need to be admired?
The rich young man had many things, but when confronted with the call to follow Christ, he could not let go of the thing standing between him and wholehearted surrender.
Then Peter spoke.
And Peter's question sounded painfully familiar.
“Behold, we have forsaken all, and followed thee; what shall we have therefore?” (Matthew 19:27, KJV).
In other words:
Lord, we gave up everything. What do we get?

Jesus did not rebuke the disciples for recognizing that sacrifice matters. He promised them a glorious future and assured them that those who left things behind for His name would receive His reward and inherit eternal life.
But immediately afterward, He said something that should make every believer examine the motives behind their obedience.
“But many that are first shall be last; and the last shall be first.” (Matthew 19:30, KJV).
Why would Jesus say that immediately after promising rewards?
Because there is a dangerous difference between serving God out of love and beginning to believe that our service gives us a claim over Him.
There is a difference between gratitude for grace and entitlement to grace.
And Jesus was about to tell a parable that would reveal just how easily the human heart confuses the two.
A landowner went out early in the morning to hire laborers for his vineyard.
Some began working at the first hour, approximately six in the morning.
Others were hired around nine.
Others at noon.
Others around three in the afternoon.
Then, at approximately five o'clock, when the working day was almost over, the landowner found still more people standing idle.
He asked why they had been standing there all day.
They answered, “Because no man hath hired us.” (Matthew 20:7, KJV).
Think about those words.
Nobody hired us.
They had been waiting.
Overlooked.
Unchosen.
Perhaps watching other men leave with the dignity of employment while they remained behind, wondering whether they would return home with anything to feed their families.
Jesus does not tell us everything about their circumstances. We should not invent their personal histories.
But He does tell us something important.
They were still there.
And the landowner invited them into his vineyard.
Even at the eleventh hour.
Even when the day was nearly finished.
Even when their opportunity appeared almost gone.
Then evening came.
The landowner instructed his steward to pay the laborers, beginning with those hired last.
And something extraordinary happened.
The men who worked only about one hour received a full denarius—the same amount originally agreed upon with those who had worked the entire day.
Imagine the surprise.
Imagine the relief.
Imagine what that payment could mean to a household that had been expecting almost nothing.
But now look at the workers who had been there since morning.
They watched the latecomers receive a denarius.
And naturally, they expected more.
After all, they had worked longer.
They had endured the heat.
They had carried the heavier burden of the day.
Surely their payment would reflect the difference.
But when their turn came, they also received a denarius.
Exactly what they had agreed to receive.
And suddenly, what had seemed fair that morning felt offensive by evening.
Not because their wages had been reduced.
But because someone else had been treated generously.
That is where the parable reaches into the deepest chambers of the human heart.
The workers complained.
“These last have wrought but one hour, and thou hast made them equal unto us, which have borne the burden and heat of the day.” (Matthew 20:12, KJV).
You made them equal to us.
There it is.
The sentence that exposes the scandal.
They were not merely upset about the money.
They were offended by the equality of the payment.
They wanted their longer labor to establish their superiority over those who came later.
And the landowner answered:
“Friend, I do thee no wrong: didst not thou agree with me for a penny?” (Matthew 20:13, KJV).
The word “penny” in the King James Version refers to a Roman denarius, commonly used as a day's wage for a laborer. It was not a modern one-cent coin.
Then the landowner asked the question that unlocks the entire parable.
“Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” (Matthew 20:15, KJV).
Read that final question again.
Is your eye evil because I am good?
In the Greek text, the words are:
ἢ ὁ ὀφθαλμός σου πονηρός ἐστιν ὅτι ἐγὼ ἀγαθός εἰμι;
Ē ho ophthalmos sou ponēros estin hoti egō agathos eimi?
Literally, the question asks whether the person's eye is evil because the landowner is good.
The expression “evil eye” belongs to a biblical world in which the eye could represent a person's inner attitude, including envy, greed, or a grudging spirit.
Here, the contrast is unmistakable.
The landowner is generous.
The complaining worker is envious.
The problem is not that goodness has failed.
The problem is that someone cannot bear to see goodness extended to another.
And suddenly this is no longer merely a story about ancient vineyard workers.
It is about us.
It is about the Christian who struggles to celebrate when a former addict begins following Jesus.
It is about the church member who resents seeing a new believer welcomed after years of rebellion.
It is about the person who secretly thinks, I have suffered too much, sacrificed too much, and obeyed too long for that person to stand beside me.
It is about the quiet bitterness that sometimes grows when God blesses someone whose story looks messier than ours.
And it is about the terrible possibility that we can be physically close to the things of God while emotionally distant from the generosity of His heart.
Jesus concludes:
“So the last shall be first, and the first last: for many be called, but few chosen.” (Matthew 20:16, KJV).

The final clause appears in the traditional Greek text underlying the King James Version, while many modern critical editions omit it from this verse because of differences among ancient manuscripts. The central statement about the first and last is secure in the textual tradition and directly connects the parable to Matthew 19:30.
In Greek, the central words read:
Οὕτως ἔσονται οἱ ἔσχατοι πρῶτοι καὶ οἱ πρῶτοι ἔσχατοι.
Houtōs esontai hoi eschatoi prōtoi kai hoi prōtoi eschatoi.
“So the last will be first, and the first last.”
The word ἔσχατοι (eschatoi) means “last,” while πρῶτοι (prōtoi) means “first.”
Jesus is deliberately reversing the order people expect.
But we must understand what He is—and is not—teaching.
He is not saying that faithfulness is worthless.
He is not teaching that laziness is spiritually superior to diligence.
He is not encouraging people to delay repentance until their final moments.
And He is certainly not teaching that everyone receives eternal life regardless of repentance and faith in Christ.
The point is more searching than that.
God's generosity cannot be controlled by human calculations of status, seniority, or deservingness.
The parable is not a complete formula for how every heavenly reward will be distributed. Jesus elsewhere teaches that faithful service matters and that God judges justly.
Rather, this story confronts the presumption that our labor makes us entitled to look down on others or dictate how generous God may be.
And the wider context makes that warning especially powerful.
The rich young man had impressive possessions and outward respectability, yet walked away from Jesus.
The disciples had truly sacrificed to follow Christ, yet needed to guard their hearts against turning that sacrifice into spiritual entitlement.
The vineyard workers received what was promised, yet some resented the master's generosity toward others.
Different situations.
One penetrating question.
Do you want God Himself, or do you want the status you think serving God should give you?
And there is another scene in Scripture that makes this even more personal.
A criminal was dying beside Jesus.
He had no years of Christian ministry to present.
No decades of faithful church attendance.
No opportunity to rebuild his reputation.
No time to demonstrate a long record of transformed behavior.
He acknowledged his guilt and recognized Jesus' innocence.
Then he said:
“Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom.” (Luke 23:42, KJV).
And Jesus answered:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.” (Luke 23:43, KJV).
A dying criminal received a promise of paradise from the crucified Savior.
Not because his crimes were insignificant.
Not because repentance was unnecessary.
Not because Jesus overlooked evil.
But because the Savior beside him had come to save sinners.

The thief's story is not another telling of the vineyard parable. Yet it beautifully illustrates the same astonishing truth: a person who comes to Christ at the end of life is not beyond the reach of His mercy.
Now imagine someone saying:
That is not fair. I have followed God for fifty years. He turned to Jesus at the very end.
But consider what those words reveal.
Would we rather see a sinner perish than see grace reach someone later than it reached us?
Have we forgotten that we, too, needed mercy?
Because whether you came to Christ at seventeen or seventy-seven, your salvation rests on the same Savior.
Jesus Christ.
The sinless Son of God.
Crucified for sinners.
Risen from the dead.
The One through whom forgiveness and reconciliation with God are offered.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
And verse 10 immediately reminds us that believers are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
That order matters.
Good works are the fruit of salvation, not the price we pay to purchase it.
We do not obey to make Jesus owe us eternal life.
We obey because the One who saved us is worthy of our love, trust, and surrender.
And this changes everything.
Because some of you reading this have been the early workers.
You have served faithfully while others disappeared.
You have prayed through painful seasons.
You have given when money was tight.
You have cared for people who never thanked you.
You have remained in ministry when your heart was exhausted.
And perhaps, deep down, you are wondering whether God has noticed.
He has.
Scripture says God is not unjust to forget the work and love shown in service to His people (Hebrews 6:10).
Jesus did not condemn the early workers for working all day.
Their labor was real.
Their burden was real.
Their agreed payment was real.
The warning came when they allowed comparison to poison their hearts.
Please hear this carefully.
You do not need to minimize your sacrifice to celebrate someone else's restoration.
You do not need to deny your suffering to rejoice when another sinner receives mercy.
And you do not need to become bitter because God has been generous to someone whose journey looks different from yours.
His goodness toward another person does not diminish His goodness toward you.
But perhaps you are not the early worker.
Perhaps you are the person who feels like you arrived too late.
You spent years running from God.
You broke promises.
You damaged relationships.
You made decisions that still keep you awake at night.
You carry memories you wish you could erase.
You see other believers with years of testimony, Scripture knowledge, and faithful service, and you wonder whether there is still a place for someone like you.
You hear them talk about their spiritual victories while you are still trying to find the courage to confess what happened yesterday.
And sometimes you whisper:
Jesus, would You still receive me?
Listen.
The vineyard parable does not promise that everyone can postpone repentance without consequence. Life is uncertain, and Scripture calls us to respond to God today.
But it does destroy the lie that your late arrival makes Christ unwilling to receive you.
Jesus said:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (John 6:37, KJV).
That promise is not reserved for people with respectable histories.
It is spoken by the Savior who receives those who come to Him.
Not because sin does not matter.
But because His grace is greater than our ability to save ourselves.
And here is where the Gospel becomes even more astonishing.
The One who told the story of the vineyard workers was Himself walking toward the cross.
In Matthew's Gospel, shortly after this parable, Jesus again foretells His betrayal, condemnation, crucifixion, and resurrection (Matthew 20:17–19).
Then He declares why He came:
“Even as the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.” (Matthew 20:28, KJV).
Do you see the beauty of that connection?
The King who overturns our obsession with being first came not to be served, but to serve.
The Lord of glory humbled Himself.
The sinless Savior took the place of sinners.
The One worthy of all honor endured the shame of the cross.
And through His death and resurrection, He opened the way for undeserving people to be reconciled to God.
The Gospel is not the announcement that God has decided sin does not matter.
The cross announces just how seriously sin matters.
And just how far divine love went to rescue sinners.
Romans 5:8 declares:
“But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us.”
While we were still sinners.
Not after we became impressive.
Not after we repaired every consequence.
Not after we proved we were better than everyone else.
Christ died for sinners.
And that is why no redeemed person has the right to boast as though salvation were a trophy earned through personal superiority.
There is room for gratitude.
There is room for worship.
There is room for faithful obedience.
But there is no room for spiritual arrogance at the foot of the cross.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question of all is this:
Would you still rejoice in God's grace if He gave it generously to someone you secretly believe deserves it less than you?
The person who betrayed your trust.
The person whose scandal embarrassed your family.
The person who once ridiculed your faith.
The person who hurt you and never fully understood the damage.
This does not mean their actions were harmless.
It does not mean repentance removes every earthly consequence.
It does not mean you must restore unsafe relationships, abandon wise boundaries, or pretend justice no longer matters.
Forgiveness, reconciliation, accountability, and restored trust are related, but they are not identical.
Yet it does mean that no sinner is beyond God's power to redeem.
And if that person genuinely turns to Christ, can you acknowledge the goodness of God without denying the seriousness of what happened?
That is not an easy question.
Sometimes the most difficult evidence of spiritual maturity is not how loudly we worship when God blesses us.
It is whether we can worship when He shows mercy to someone we would have preferred to see rejected.
Remember the older brother in Jesus' parable of the prodigal son.
He remained at home.
He worked.
He obeyed.
But when his younger brother returned after squandering his inheritance, the older brother became angry and refused to join the celebration (Luke 15:25–30).
His father went out and pleaded with him.
And the father said:
“It was meet that we should make merry, and be glad: for this thy brother was dead, and is alive again; and was lost, and is found.” (Luke 15:32, KJV).
The older brother was so focused on what his brother had received that he struggled to celebrate what his father had restored.
He was near the father's house.
But in that moment, his heart was far from the father's joy.
That is the danger Jesus is exposing.
You can be near religious activity and still resist the heart of grace.
You can know the language of righteousness and still be controlled by envy.
You can spend years doing outwardly good things while quietly turning your obedience into a reason to despise others.
And when that happens, the answer is not to stop obeying.
The answer is to repent.
To return to Christ.
To ask Him to cleanse not only our visible behavior but also our hidden motives.
Because grace does not merely welcome the scandalous sinner.
It also confronts the proud saint.
It humbles both.
And it invites both to find their hope in Jesus alone.
Maybe that is why these words are so unforgettable.
“The last shall be first, and the first last.”
They are not simply a comforting slogan for people who feel overlooked.
They are a warning against presumption.
A rebuke to envy.
A challenge to spiritual pride.
And a beautiful reminder that God's Kingdom does not operate according to the status games we play on earth.
The person everyone applauds may desperately need repentance.
The person everyone has written off may be turning toward Jesus with genuine faith.
The believer with decades of service must still depend on grace.
The new convert has no reason to despair because of a late beginning.
And every one of us must remember that Christ, not our religious résumé, is our only Savior.
So do not use this parable to delay your surrender.
Do not say, I will come to Jesus when I am old. I will live however I want and seek forgiveness at the eleventh hour.
The thief on the cross received mercy, but Scripture never promises you another hour.
Today is the day to turn to Christ.
And do not use your years of service as permission to become proud.
If you have followed Jesus for decades, praise God for His sustaining grace.
If you have only recently come to Him, praise God for His receiving grace.
If you have wandered and need to return, do not make peace with the darkness.
Come back to the Savior.
Confess your sin.
Turn from it.
Trust in His finished work.
Follow Him.
Because the purpose of grace is not to leave us unchanged.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Real grace does not make repentance unnecessary.
Real grace leads us toward the One who transforms us.
And that brings us to the heart of Gospel Warrior.
Not because Jesus pretends the scandal never happened.
Not because consequences automatically disappear.
Not because the past becomes acceptable simply because someone has found religion.
But because Jesus can redeem what sin has devastated.
He can forgive the guilty.
Humble the proud.
Restore the repentant.
Give hope to the ashamed.
And create a new life where there was once spiritual death.
That is the Gospel we want to keep proclaiming.
Not a Gospel that flatters the religious.
Not a Gospel that excuses rebellion.
Not a Gospel that sells blessings to the highest bidder.
But the biblical Gospel of Jesus Christ—crucified, risen, reigning, and mighty to save.
And if these words have exposed something in you, please do not rush past that conviction.
Maybe you have been comparing your journey with someone else's.
Maybe you have secretly resented another person's restoration.
Maybe you have been trying to earn God's acceptance through endless religious activity.
Or maybe you have spent so long believing you are too late that you have almost stopped hoping.
Bring that honestly before Jesus.
And if this message has challenged you to surrender the pride, comparison, or hidden sin you have been carrying, you can simply write “no more hiding.”
Let it become a moment of honest reflection before God.
And please, think of someone who needs this message.
Someone who has given up on church because they feel judged.
Someone who believes their past has disqualified them from God's mercy.
Someone who has faithfully served for years but is quietly becoming bitter.
Someone whose family is still praying for their return to Christ.
A simple share can put a Gospel message before someone who would never have searched for it.
Not as a spiritual good-luck charm, but as a reminder to return to Matthew 19 and 20 whenever comparison, discouragement, or pride begins to distort your understanding of grace.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people grow beyond the emotional moment of reading an article.
We want to help believers open their Bibles, understand the Gospel, examine their hearts, and become more faithful disciples of Jesus Christ.
We believe biblical nourishment should be accessible, especially to people who are hungry for truth but may not have the means to purchase every resource they need.
And that ongoing work requires real support.
Writing, publishing, developing resources, maintaining a growing library, and expanding Gospel-centered outreach all involve time, labor, and practical expenses.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV).
And no amount of money can purchase salvation, forgiveness, spiritual maturity, or a special place in His Kingdom.
But generous, willing support can be a beautiful expression of Christian partnership.
Philippians 4:15–18 shows believers participating in the work of Gospel ministry through material generosity.
The greatest purpose is not merchandise.
It is the message.
It is the possibility of another person encountering the Gospel.
Another struggling believer being encouraged to return to Scripture.
Another ashamed sinner discovering that repentance and forgiveness are possible through Jesus Christ.
Another family receiving resources that help them grow in faith.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage someone.
Use the free resources.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your worth before God or your place in this community.
And perhaps that is one more way this very parable should shape our ministry.
We must never preach the generosity of God's grace while treating people as though their financial contributions determine their spiritual importance.
The longtime believer is welcome.
The new believer is welcome.
The wounded seeker who is still asking questions is welcome to listen, learn, and explore the claims of Jesus Christ.
Because the vineyard belongs to the Master.
The Gospel belongs to Christ.
And the glory belongs to God.
One day, the applause of this world will fade.
The titles will disappear.
The numbers on our screens will no longer matter.
The arguments about who was more important, more impressive, or more deserving will sound painfully small in the presence of the Lord.
What will matter is whether we truly belong to Jesus Christ.
Whether our hope was in His grace rather than our own righteousness.
Whether our faith bore the fruit of love and obedience.
Whether we learned to rejoice in the mercy that rescued us instead of resenting the mercy that rescued someone else.
And perhaps the person standing beside you in God's Kingdom will have a story you never expected to hear.
A former enemy.
A notorious sinner.
Someone you thought would never repent.
Someone who came to Jesus much later than you did.
And if you are both there through the saving work of Christ, the right response will not be to ask why they were welcomed.
It will be to worship the Savior who was merciful enough to welcome either of you.
Because heaven is not a competition between people who think they deserve to be there.
It is the home of those redeemed by Jesus Christ.
And when you finally understand how much grace it took to save you, you will stop being offended by how much grace God shows to someone else.
The greatest tragedy would not be arriving last at the vineyard—it would be standing inside it, surrounded by the Master's goodness, and never learning to rejoice in His grace.
